First Pass: opa data - philadelphia_sfh_modeling.csv¶

Run Timestamp: 2026-10-04 16:38:19 First Pass Version: 1.1.0

Key Takeaways¶

  • Robust Out-of-Time Valuation Framework: The modeling handoff establishes a clean temporal holdout (64,336 sales from 2020–mid 2025 vs. 5,030 sales in H1 2026), providing an isolated benchmark to test model generalization and track post-2025 price trajectory without data leakage.
  • Physical Scale and Layout Efficiency as Core Valuation Anchors: Usable living area (log_livable_area) represents the primary continuous driver of property value, while parcel density (FAR) and balanced bed-to-bath configurations create distinct non-linear premiums across Philadelphia's dominant row and twin home typologies.
  • High Capitalization of Modernization Over Vintage: While construction era sets baseline depreciation, condition ratings and modernized mechanical systems (specifically central air conditioning) command significant value premiums, demonstrating that effective maintenance and renovations heavily offset chronological age.
  • Marked Geographic Price Divergence: Substantial price variance across OPA Geographic Market Area (GMA) zones and neighborhoods highlights hyper-local market segmentation as a non-negotiable stratification layer for equitable property modeling.
  • Municipal Assessment-to-Market Discrepancies: Comparing market transactions against published TY2025 and TY2027 OPA assessments reveals critical ratios and valuation lags, offering clear targets for correcting systematic over- or under-assessment across submarkets.
  • Repeat-Sales Validation Opportunity: The presence of 1,075 repeat-sale parcels bridging the training and holdout periods offers an empirical baseline to measure pure parcel-level appreciation and calibrate time-trend adjustments (time_years_from_2027).

Input Summary¶

  • File: C:\Users\arvin\Desktop\Sample Datasets\opa data - philadelphia_sfh_modeling.csv
  • Shape: 69366 rows, 44 columns
  • User Input: # Philadelphia single-family modeling handoff

Start with philadelphia_sfh_modeling.csv. It has 69,366 sale observations and 44 columns, exported from the active sfh-pwd-v4 pipeline without further cleaning or imputation. It contains the exact headline TY2027 modeling cohorts, not the full city inventory or every sale since 2020.

  • Training: 64,336 sales, January 1, 2020–June 30, 2025.
  • Holdout: 5,030 sales, January 1–June 30, 2026.
  • July–December 2025 is deliberately absent in this particular assessment-cycle comparison.
  • One retained sale per parcel within each window; 1,075 holdout parcels also appear in training. IDs are unique within split, not necessarily across the whole file. This is a time holdout, not an exclusively new-parcel holdout.
  • No names of buyers/sellers, model predictions, or risk-classifier scores are included.

How to start¶

Use observed_price for a dollar-price model or log_price for a log-price model. Never include the other target as a predictor. feature_lists.json lists the exact current headline property inputs. Include time_years_from_2027 for a direct-time model. The direct LightGBM recipe handles time separately; an ordinary tree with time as another input will not reproduce its extrapolation. Published assessments are optional benchmarks, not inputs to our headline models. Likewise exclude split, ID, address and parcel_in_training from features.

For a first benchmark, fit log_price on property features and time with numeric variables plus one-hot categorical variables. Train only on split=train; evaluate split=test at each observed sale month. For Jan2027 assessments set time to zero, but comparing those predictions to raw2026 sales mixes prediction error with the difference in dates. Preprocessing, category encoding and tuning should use training data only.

This export does not supply TASP: it would require an explicitly chosen index/anchor and training-only estimation. Neither observed_price nor log_price is time-adjusted. Demographic variables are not included in this basic handoff.

Data provenance and limits¶

Sales come from the cached Philadelphia deed data; property characteristics and published assessments from OPA; selected lot measurements use PWD parcel checks; neighborhood categories use the project's Zillow boundary assignment. Features describe the current retained inventory and may postdate historical sales. This is not a collection of historical property snapshots.

The shared pipeline restricts records to supported single-family homes, excluding condos and unresolved property/measurement conflicts. It retains the latest transaction within each window before applying single-property, minimum-price, party/distress and measurement checks. It also applies training-derived 2nd/99.9th percentile price limits ($40,000–$2,475,000) to both cohorts. It is therefore a screened sample, not all transactions or a representative sample of every home. The cached records may be incomplete. These test periods have been inspected during prior research.

No new values were imputed in this export. Raw OPA area fields remain beside selected model area fields. Recorded numeric zeros remain zero. Categorical MISSING is an explicit category; blank CSV fields are missing values. Some source categories are numeric-looking codes—treat them as nominal. Read parcel identifiers as strings, preserving leading zeros. Square footage is square feet; prices are dollars. Do not assume OPA year built is historically accurate.

Published TY2027 assessments are retained for comparison; they are not observed ground truth. The CSV does not estimate taxes or contain the unsold-parcel prediction population.

Reading in Python¶

import json
import pandas as pd
d = pd.read_csv('philadelphia_sfh_modeling.csv',
                dtype={'opa_parcel_number': str},
                keep_default_na=False, na_values=[''])
d['document_date'] = pd.to_datetime(d['document_date'])
spec = json.load(open('feature_lists.json'))
for c in spec['categorical']:
    d[c] = d[c].astype('category')
train = d[d['split'] == 'train'].copy()
test = d[d['split'] == 'test'].copy()

Column dictionary¶

Column Meaning
opa_parcel_number OPA account identifier; read as text. Identifier, not a predictor.
split train = Jan2020–Jun2025; test = Jan–Jun2026. Preserve for our chronological comparison.
document_date Recorded transaction date, ISO YYYY-MM-DD.
observed_price Observed deed consideration in USD after transaction screening. Not TASP and not a model prediction.
log_price Natural log of observed_price. Alternative target; never a feature when predicting price.
log_livable_area Natural log of model_livable_area.
log_land_area Natural log of model_land_area.
garage_spaces Recorded garage-space count.
number_of_bedrooms Recorded bedroom count.
number_of_bathrooms Recorded bathroom count.
number_stories Recorded number of stories.
both_room_counts_zero 1 when recorded bedrooms and bathrooms are both zero, else 0. Zeros were not imputed.
far model_livable_area / model_land_area. Floor-area-ratio proxy.
building_code_description_new Current OPA property-style description category.
era_built Provisional construction-era category derived from OPA year built.
interior_condition Normalized OPA interior condition category/code; nominal, not an ordinal numeric scale.
central_air Normalized OPA central air category/code; nominal, not an ordinal numeric scale.
view_type Normalized OPA view type category/code; nominal, not an ordinal numeric scale.
gma Fine OPA Geographic Market Area category.
exterior_condition Normalized OPA exterior condition category/code; nominal, not an ordinal numeric scale.
basements Normalized OPA basements category/code; nominal, not an ordinal numeric scale.
type_heater Normalized OPA type heater category/code; nominal, not an ordinal numeric scale.
general_construction Normalized OPA general construction category/code; nominal, not an ordinal numeric scale.
parcel_shape Normalized OPA parcel shape category/code; nominal, not an ordinal numeric scale.
topography Normalized OPA topography category/code; nominal, not an ordinal numeric scale.
gma_group Intermediate OPA GMA grouping category.
gma_zone Broad OPA modeling zone category; used for stratification.
neighborhood_name Zillow neighborhood category.
street_address OPA location label; audit/reference only, not used as predictor.
land_area Recorded OPA lot area, square feet; retained separately from selected model measurement.
livable_area Recorded OPA living area, square feet.
model_land_area Selected model lot area in square feet, including supported PWD corrections.
model_livable_area Selected supported living area in square feet.
land_area_source Provenance of selected land measurement.
land_area_check Land measurement consistency classification.
year_built Recorded OPA year built; often approximate; reference field, not our numeric predictor.
year_built_estimate OPA construction-year estimate indicator, retained as recorded.
garage_type Recorded garage type category; used in OPA-style comparisons, not headline direct model.
geocode_lat Latitude supplied in inventory; not a current headline predictor.
geocode_long Longitude supplied in inventory; not a current headline predictor.
time_years_from_2027 ((year−2027)*12+month−1)/12. Monthly-resolution numeric trend; set to zero for Jan2027 predictions.
parcel_in_training Whether this parcel appears in training; always true for training rows. Identifies repeat parcels in holdout.
published_opa_2025 Published TY2025 assessment, USD. Optional benchmark; excluded from our predictors.
published_opa_2027 Published TY2027 assessment, USD. Optional benchmark; excluded from our predictors and unavailable at historical cutoff.

except Exception as e:

Error saving dataset: row index was 65536, not allowed by .xls format

Insight: The automated serialization pipeline failed during legacy Excel (.xls) generation because the dataset's 69,366 rows exceed the format's hard limit of 65,536 rows. While modern formats like Parquet and standard CSV succeed, analytical pipelines must avoid legacy binary spreadsheets to prevent truncation and pipeline crashes.

Section 2: Macro Temporal Trends & Cohort Dynamics: Trajectory from 2020 through 2026 Holdout¶

Examines property appreciation trajectory over time, validating the structural stability between the training cohort (2020-2025) and the forward holdout evaluation window (2026).

Step Columns Template Rationale Playbooks
1 document_date, observed_price, split custom_code Establishes baseline macro inflation and seasonal volume patterns, evaluating whether holdout sales in 2026 align with long-term price trajectories or reflect regime shifts. custom_code
2 log_price, split custom_code Identifies distributional shift in target variable log_price between training and holdout datasets to calibrate model generalization expectations. custom_code

Section 3: Physical Scale & Density Levers: Living Area, Parcel Footprint, and Typology¶

Quantifies the elasticity of sale price with respect to livable area, parcel dimensions, floor-area ratio, and architectural building styles.

Step Columns Template Rationale Playbooks
1 log_livable_area, log_price, building_code_description_new custom_code Livable area is the primary continuous physical driver; evaluating its slope across key row and twin typologies reveals segment-specific baseline valuation scales. custom_code
2 far, number_of_bedrooms, number_of_bathrooms, log_price custom_code Uncovers non-linear land density premiums and highlights high-value room configurations to identify asset utility bottlenecks. custom_code

Section 4: Condition, Quality, and Vintage Premiums: Depreciation and Renovation Returns¶

Evaluates valuation increments associated with property construction vintage, interior/exterior condition codes, and HVAC modernization.

Step Columns Template Rationale Playbooks
1 era_built, interior_condition, observed_price custom_code Isolates the condition premium across vintages to determine whether physical degradation or historical vintage poses the dominant appraisal penalty. custom_code
2 central_air, era_built, log_price custom_code Quantifies the capitalization of modern HVAC systems in older Philadelphia housing stock versus contemporary builds. custom_code

Section 5: Geographic Stratification & Assessment Audit: Zone Discrepancies and OPA Ratios¶

Investigates submarket spatial variation across OPA GMA zones and audits actual market transactions against published TY2025 and TY2027 OPA assessments.

Step Columns Template Rationale Playbooks

2 observed_price, published_opa_2025, published_opa_2027, split custom_code Audits published municipal tax assessments against real market clearing prices to assess over- and under-assessment skews across train and holdout windows. custom_code

2. Macro Temporal Trends & Cohort Dynamics: Trajectory from 2020 through 2026 Holdout¶

Examines property appreciation trajectory over time, validating the structural stability between the training cohort (2020-2025) and the forward holdout evaluation window (2026).

How have transaction prices and market volume trended from 2020 through the 2026 holdout period?¶

Establishes baseline macro inflation and seasonal volume patterns, evaluating whether holdout sales in 2026 align with long-term price trajectories or reflect regime shifts.

In [14]:
try:
    fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6))
    df_temp = df.copy()
    df_temp['month_yr'] = pd.to_datetime(df_temp['document_date']).dt.to_period('M')
    monthly = df_temp.groupby('month_yr').agg(median_price=('observed_price', 'median'), volume=('observed_price', 'count')).reset_index()
    monthly['month_dt'] = monthly['month_yr'].dt.to_timestamp()
    ax2 = ax1.twinx()
    ax2.bar(monthly['month_dt'], monthly['volume'], width=20, alpha=0.25, color='gray', label='Monthly Volume')
    ax1.plot(monthly['month_dt'], monthly['median_price'], color='#1f77b4', linewidth=2.5, marker='o', label='Median Price ($)')
    ax1.axvline(pd.Timestamp('2025-06-30'), color='#d62728', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label='Train/Holdout Boundary')
    ax1.set_xlabel('Sale Date')
    ax1.set_ylabel('Median Observed Price ($)', color='#1f77b4')
    ax2.set_ylabel('Transaction Volume', color='gray')
    plt.title('Philadelphia Single-Family Price Trajectory and Transaction Volume (2020 - 2026)')
    ax1.grid(True, linestyle=':', alpha=0.6)
    h1, l1 = ax1.get_legend_handles_labels()
    h2, l2 = ax2.get_legend_handles_labels()
    ax1.legend(h1 + h2, l1 + l2, loc='upper left')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: Monthly transaction volumes and median prices display pronounced seasonality, peaking mid-year and dipping during winter troughs, alongside a steep price escalation into early 2026. The temporal boundary split at June 30, 2025 creates a realistic out-of-time test scenario, demanding that predictive models account for inflation and market velocity shifts to avoid systematically underestimating future property values.

Does the log price target distribution drift significantly between the training and test holdout cohorts?¶

Identifies distributional shift in target variable log_price between training and holdout datasets to calibrate model generalization expectations.

In [7]:
try:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5)); sns.kdeplot(data=df, x='log_price', hue='split', common_norm=False, fill=True, alpha=0.35, palette={'train': '#2ca02c', 'test': '#ff7f0e'}, ax=ax); train_med = df[df['split']=='train']['log_price'].median(); test_med = df[df['split']=='test']['log_price'].median(); ax.axvline(train_med, color='#2ca02c', linestyle='--', label=f'Train Median ({train_med:.2f})'); ax.axvline(test_med, color='#ff7f0e', linestyle='--', label=f'Test Median ({test_med:.2f})'); ax.set_title('Target Density Comparison: Log Price in Train vs Test Splits'); ax.set_xlabel('Natural Log of Observed Price'); ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout();
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: The natural log price distribution exhibits a slight rightward shift from train (median 12.37) to test (median 12.45), corroborating continuing real estate appreciation across Philadelphia. Ensuring close distributional alignment between splits confirms the absence of extreme structural drift, validating the out-of-time partition for measuring actual model generalizability.

3. Physical Scale & Density Levers: Living Area, Parcel Footprint, and Typology¶

Quantifies the elasticity of sale price with respect to livable area, parcel dimensions, floor-area ratio, and architectural building styles.

What is the structural relationship and elasticity between living area and log price across top building types?¶

Livable area is the primary continuous physical driver; evaluating its slope across key row and twin typologies reveals segment-specific baseline valuation scales.

In [8]:
try:
    top_styles = df['building_code_description_new'].value_counts().nlargest(4).index; sub = df[df['building_code_description_new'].isin(top_styles)].copy(); g = sns.lmplot(data=sub, x='log_livable_area', y='log_price', hue='building_code_description_new', col='building_code_description_new', col_wrap=2, height=4, aspect=1.3, scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.15, 's': 10}, line_kws={'color': 'darkred'}); g.set_axis_labels('Log Livable Area (sq ft)', 'Log Observed Price'); g.set_titles(col_template='{col_name}'); plt.subplots_adjust(top=0.9); g.fig.suptitle('Marginal Price Elasticity by Primary Building Style');
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: Log-log regressions between living area and transaction price reveal consistent, positive marginal price elasticity across the top four residential building archetypes. The steeper price slope in ROW TYPICAL and ROW POST WAR properties indicates that living space expansion yields a higher marginal return in attached urban configurations than in semi-detached conventional twins.

How does parcel utilization (Floor-to-Area Ratio) and bedroom/bathroom configurations dictate unit value?¶

Uncovers non-linear land density premiums and highlights high-value room configurations to identify asset utility bottlenecks.

In [9]:
try:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5)); sub = df[(df['far'] <= 3.0) & (df['number_of_bedrooms'] <= 5) & (df['number_of_bathrooms'] <= 4)].copy(); sns.scatterplot(data=sub.sample(min(5000, len(sub))), x='far', y='log_price', alpha=0.3, ax=ax1, color='#34495e'); sns.regplot(data=sub, x='far', y='log_price', scatter=False, ax=ax1, color='red'); ax1.set_title('Log Price vs Floor Area Ratio (FAR <= 3)'); ax1.set_xlabel('FAR (Living Area / Land Area)'); ax1.set_ylabel('Log Price'); pvt = sub.groupby(['number_of_bedrooms', 'number_of_bathrooms'])['log_price'].median().unstack(); sns.heatmap(pvt, cmap='YlGnBu', annot=True, fmt='.2f', ax=ax2, cbar_kws={'label': 'Median Log Price'}); ax2.set_title('Median Log Price by Bed/Bath Matrix'); ax2.set_xlabel('Number of Bathrooms'); ax2.set_ylabel('Number of Bedrooms'); plt.tight_layout();
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: Floor Area Ratio (FAR) demonstrates a modest positive correlation with price, indicating that denser parcel utilization yields higher value despite diminishing returns at extreme ratios. Concurrently, the bedroom-bathroom matrix highlights that adding bathrooms drives higher median valuation gains than bedroom count alone, serving as a stronger proxy for modern renovations and luxury tiers.

4. Condition, Quality, and Vintage Premiums: Depreciation and Renovation Returns¶

Evaluates valuation increments associated with property construction vintage, interior/exterior condition codes, and HVAC modernization.

What valuation premium is commanded across construction eras and interior condition tiers?¶

Isolates the condition premium across vintages to determine whether physical degradation or historical vintage poses the dominant appraisal penalty.

In [10]:
try:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6)); era_order = sorted(df['era_built'].dropna().unique()); cond_summary = df[df['interior_condition'].isin([2, 3, 4, 5, 6])].groupby(['era_built', 'interior_condition'])['observed_price'].median().reset_index(); sns.barplot(data=cond_summary, x='era_built', y='observed_price', hue='interior_condition', palette='Blues', order=era_order, ax=ax); ax.set_title('Median Observed Price by Era Built and Interior Condition Rating'); ax.set_xlabel('Construction Era'); ax.set_ylabel('Median Price ($)'); ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter('${x:,.0f}'); ax.legend(title='Interior Condition', loc='upper left'); plt.xticks(rotation=30); plt.tight_layout();
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: Modern construction (2000+) commands premium valuation tiers, but interior condition ratings create significant valuation divergence across every construction vintage. Notably, prime condition ratings (2–3) in historic pre-1940 structures achieve parity with mid-century builds, underscoring that renovation status is a dominant price lever comparable to structural age.

Does central air conditioning provide a consistent price uplift across different eras of construction?¶

Quantifies the capitalization of modern HVAC systems in older Philadelphia housing stock versus contemporary builds.

In [11]:
try:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5)); ac_df = df[df['central_air'].isin(['Y', 'N'])].copy(); sns.boxplot(data=ac_df, x='era_built', y='log_price', hue='central_air', palette={'Y': '#2ecc71', 'N': '#e74c3c'}, showfliers=False, ax=ax); ax.set_title('Central Air HVAC Premium on Log Price Across Building Eras'); ax.set_xlabel('Era Built'); ax.set_ylabel('Log Observed Price'); ax.legend(title='Central Air'); plt.xticks(rotation=25); plt.tight_layout();
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: Across every historical era, central air conditioning confers a consistent valuation premium, visible in the upward shift of median log prices. The effect is most pronounced in pre-1940 housing stock, where the presence of modern HVAC signals comprehensive capital improvements and electrical modernizations.

5. Geographic Stratification & Assessment Audit: Zone Discrepancies and OPA Ratios¶

Investigates submarket spatial variation across OPA GMA zones and audits actual market transactions against published TY2025 and TY2027 OPA assessments.

Which GMA modeling zones exhibit the highest price dispersion and valuation levels?¶

Establishes the primary geographic stratification baselines used by city assessors to verify market uniformity and spatial divergence.

In [12]:
try:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6)); zone_order = df.groupby('gma_zone')['observed_price'].median().sort_values(ascending=False).index; sns.boxplot(data=df, x='gma_zone', y='observed_price', order=zone_order, hue='gma_zone', legend=False, palette='viridis', showfliers=False, ax=ax); ax.set_title('Observed Price Distribution Across OPA GMA Zones (Ordered by Median)'); ax.set_xlabel('GMA Modeling Zone'); ax.set_ylabel('Observed Price ($)'); ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter('${x:,.0f}'); plt.tight_layout();
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: Geographic Modeling Area (GMA) zones exhibit massive wealth stratification, ranging from median single-family prices exceeding $600,000 in prime core zones (P, Q) to under $150,000 in outer or transitional areas (B, G). This stark geographic dispersion confirms that spatial zoning hierarchy is among the single strongest predictors of market valuation and assessment tax base allocation.

How closely do published OPA TY2025 and TY2027 assessments track observed market transaction prices?¶

Audits published municipal tax assessments against real market clearing prices to assess over- and under-assessment skews across train and holdout windows.

In [15]:
try:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6))
    df_audit = df[(df['published_opa_2025'] > 0) & (df['published_opa_2027'] > 0) & (df['observed_price'] > 0)].copy()
    df_audit['ratio_2025'] = df_audit['published_opa_2025'] / df_audit['observed_price']
    df_audit['ratio_2027'] = df_audit['published_opa_2027'] / df_audit['observed_price']

    sns.kdeplot(data=df_audit, x='ratio_2025', hue='split', common_norm=False, fill=True, alpha=0.3, ax=ax1)
    ax1.axvline(1.0, color='red', linestyle='--', label='Parity (1.0)')
    ax1.set_xlim(0.2, 2.5)
    ax1.set_title('Assessment-to-Sale Ratio (TY2025 Published OPA)')
    ax1.set_xlabel('Ratio: Published 2025 / Observed Price')
    leg1 = ax1.get_legend()
    if leg1:
        handles1 = getattr(leg1, 'legend_handles', getattr(leg1, 'legendHandles', []))
        labels1 = [t.get_text() for t in leg1.get_texts()]
        p_line = plt.Line2D([0], [0], color='red', linestyle='--', label='Parity (1.0)')
        ax1.legend(handles1 + [p_line], labels1 + ['Parity (1.0)'], loc='upper right')

    sns.kdeplot(data=df_audit, x='ratio_2027', hue='split', common_norm=False, fill=True, alpha=0.3, ax=ax2)
    ax2.axvline(1.0, color='red', linestyle='--', label='Parity (1.0)')
    ax2.set_xlim(0.2, 2.5)
    ax2.set_title('Assessment-to-Sale Ratio (TY2027 Published OPA)')
    ax2.set_xlabel('Ratio: Published 2027 / Observed Price')
    leg2 = ax2.get_legend()
    if leg2:
        handles2 = getattr(leg2, 'legend_handles', getattr(leg2, 'legendHandles', []))
        labels2 = [t.get_text() for t in leg2.get_texts()]
        p_line = plt.Line2D([0], [0], color='red', linestyle='--', label='Parity (1.0)')
        ax2.legend(handles2 + [p_line], labels2 + ['Parity (1.0)'], loc='upper right')

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: Both the TY2025 and TY2027 assessment-to-sale ratio distributions center tightly around market parity (1.0) in the training data, indicating robust calibration of published city assessments against historical transactions. However, the systematic leftward skew in the test holdout indicates that post-split price appreciation outpaced official assessments, resulting in mild systemic under-assessment in prospective tax years.
